description: We are a group of three students who love robotics, engineering, and satellites.
summary:
Burn Clock merges 548,501,203 NASA FIRMS fire detections from five satellites (MODIS on Terra and Aqua; VIIRS on S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21) into one burning-activity calendar for any place on Earth, every month since 2001, on one scale. The 2012 MODIS-to-VIIRS jump falls from x2.48 to x0.96; median error on held-out years is 1.1%.

It also catches what other fire records miss: these satellites only look at fixed times of day. In Punjab, India, the official count fell 93% from 2021 to 2025, but an hourly satellite shows afternoon burning fell only about 34%: 96% of it now happens after 4 pm, after the satellites pass. Every place gets one of four verdicts: timing matters, the old MODIS record is off, timing doesn't explain this, or can't tell yet.

Users pick their job and a place (any country, province or drawn area). Burn Clock shows the calendar, says if the trend can be trusted, compares this week's live NASA data with a normal week, and gives a plan: for Punjab, which districts to check this week and when (Fazilka: 4-6 pm). An AI Advisor answers using only our data, every number checked.

Why it matters: India's government reported a 93% drop in Punjab farm fires, and the smoke forecasts for more than 30 million people in Delhi rest on the same satellite counts. But 96% of the burning now happens when those satellites aren't looking. The real afternoon drop was about 34%, so the official number overstated the progress almost threefold.
details:
THE PROBLEM

NASA's MODIS (Terra, Aqua; since 2000) and VIIRS (S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21; since 2012) fire records cannot simply be joined: VIIRS sees many more small fires, so the record jumps in 2012. The satellites also only see each place at a few fixed times a day, and those times are changing: Terra now passes about an hour earlier and Aqua about an hour later. People change too. In Punjab, India, farmers burning rice stubble moved to late afternoon, after the ~1:30 pm passes. India reported a 93% fall in farm fires from 2021 to 2025. An hourly geostationary satellite (GK2A) shows the whole afternoon fell only about 34%; the share of afternoon burning at 4 pm or later rose from 35% (2019) to 96% (2025), while the 1-2 pm share fell from 32% to 1%. Officials, journalists and smoke forecasters read the count as "how much burning happened". When burning moves out of view, they draw the wrong conclusion.

WHAT WE BUILT

Burn Clock (https://burn-clock.vercel.app) is a free public web app.

1. What do you do? District officer, air-quality forecaster, journalist or researcher.

2. Which place? Search 176 countries and about 4,600 states and provinces with real borders, or draw a rectangle, circle or freehand shape, or click a province. Each area gets its own fire season automatically. Four one-click scenarios show all four possible verdicts.

3. Fire calendar: a world map of fire activity next to the harmonized month-by-year calendar since 2001. It shows the fire season (Punjab: Oct-Nov, 63% of a typical year), each month against the 2003-2022 average, the record by satellite, and a CSV export. A "Clock check" column marks each year since 2021 as trustworthy or distorted by satellite timing. Punjab also has a day-by-day view.

4. What should I do? Three answers, each ending in one action for the chosen job: when to act (with a calendar reminder), can you trust the trend, and how this week compares with a normal week of the same month from NASA's live data. A low count with burning moved later is never called progress.

5. Playbook by job. For Punjab: districts ranked by this week's NASA fire detections, each with the best time to check fields from the hourly satellite (Fazilka: 4-6 pm covered 99% of its afternoon burning in 2025; its satellite count fell 87% vs 21% for the whole afternoon). Officers get a team planner; forecasters get the share of burning after 4 pm to time emissions; journalists get "you can say / don't say" sentences with the numbers; researchers get data, API and tested errors. One tap sends the plan to WhatsApp. Elsewhere: this week's hotspots inside the area.

6. AI Advisor (Claude): knows the selected place, months, job and local time; can only use Burn Clock's data; the server checks every number before it is shown.

7. Live: a worldwide table of where burning is later than usual this week and a public JSON API (/api/check, /api/punjab). NASA's 7-day files are re-read every 6 hours.

HOW IT WORKS

548,501,203 NASA FIRMS detections (MODIS C6.1, VIIRS 375 m), 2001-2025, on a 0.25-degree global grid. Each MODIS satellite is converted to the VIIRS scale with factors fitted only on 2013-2019, before the orbit drift; every value has an uncertainty range. The 2012 seam falls from x2.48 to x0.96; median error on held-out years is 1.1% worldwide and 5.9% in Punjab. Two checks give each place a verdict: has burning moved to hours the satellites miss (the drifting Aqua vs fixed VIIRS), and is the older MODIS record off (Terra and Aqua vs VIIRS), each against 2013-2019 normal swings. Six case studies give four different answers; Punjab's wheat season is the built-in control.

IMPACT

Fire counts drive policy, penalties and smoke forecasts for hundreds of millions of people. Burn Clock lets a district officer send teams when fires actually burn, a forecaster time smoke correctly, a journalist report accurately, and a researcher use a consistent 25-year record with honest error bars.

CREATIVITY

Others treat satellite pass times as fixed. We use Aqua's drift as a natural experiment that reveals hidden afternoon burning anywhere on Earth, live.

VALIDITY AND HONESTY

Every number links to the file and code that produced it. An automated test gate recomputes the reference numbers on every change. Known failures are published: conversion factors don't carry between continents, the Parana Delta has about 21% held-out error, and the hourly GK2A record covers noon-6 pm only and is preliminary. The verdict is a diagnostic, not proof of why burning moved. NASA (Jethva 2026), ISRO's Space Applications Centre and iFOREST first reported the Punjab shift; we built the check for everywhere, live, with actions.

TOOLS

TypeScript, React, Vite, MapLibre GL, Python (data pipeline), Node.js, Vercel (hosting and API), GitHub Actions (live refresh), Anthropic Claude API (advisor), Playwright, Vitest and axe-core (testing and accessibility).
